Acetaminophen pharmacology: 4

A patient takes a cold remedy and a separate pain medicine, unaware both contain acetaminophen. The total exposure exceeds the intended limit. Which medication-use problem best explains this avoidable route to overdose?

  1. NAPQI-mediated hepatic injury
  2. N-acetylcysteine
  3. Serious cutaneous adverse reaction
  4. Unintentional duplicate acetaminophen exposure
  5. Analgesic and antipyretic effects with limited peripheral anti-inflammatory action
Answer and explanation

Unintentional duplicate acetaminophen exposure

Combination cold and pain products can contain acetaminophen, creating overdose risk when totals are not reconciled.

Option explanations

Unintentional duplicate acetaminophen exposure: Combination cold and pain products can contain acetaminophen, creating overdose risk when totals are not reconciled.

Analgesic and antipyretic effects with limited peripheral anti-inflammatory action: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever but does not provide the same peripheral anti-inflammatory action as conventional NSAIDs. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

NAPQI-mediated hepatic injury: Excess acetaminophen can overwhelm glutathione detoxification of the reactive metabolite NAPQI. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

N-acetylcysteine: N-acetylcysteine supports glutathione-dependent detoxification and is the antidote used for acetaminophen poisoning. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Serious cutaneous adverse reaction: Acetaminophen can rarely cause severe skin reactions, including SJS/TEN; rash with blistering or mucosal injury requires urgent assessment. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
